Haripal was born in the Jamuna-Chambal doab, and later the Gwalior tract north of the Vindhyas, a landscape where the memory of the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior was kept alive not by stone inscriptions alone, but by bards who walked from village to village, by mothers who sang lullabies of old battles, and by clan-councils held under the ancient banyan. 10th–11th century CE was an age when every fort had its own ghost, every pass its own tradition, and every shrine its own protective vow. The clan deity, Sri Krishna and the patron shrine of Gadh Govinda, was worshipped with a lamp that never went out; caravans stopped before entering the hills; and sentinels watched every waterhole through the night. It was in such a world that Haripal grew up, sitting at the knee of Ruler Tomar dynasty Ancestor and learning the first, cruel truth of Rajput kingship: that the throne is not comfort, but a vow.
Their education was deliberately rounded. The four martial sciences - bow, horse, sword, and mace - were taught before the letters of the alphabet. Then came the shastras, but never only from books. Economics was taught from the account-books of a merchant caravan. Statecraft was taught from a rebel chieftain's forgiven letter. Justice was taught from the actual hearing of a widow's land dispute in the village chaupal. Music and painting were not ornaments; they were meant to train eye and ear, so that a king could read the lie in a courtier's salute and the truth in the murmur of a crowd.
From the queen-mother, Haripal received an even more difficult lesson: a king's courage is not proven on the battlefield alone. It is proven when he listens silently to a complaint he does not want to hear, when he feeds the hungry before his own table, when he keeps his word to a weaker ally even if every minister advises him otherwise. These quiet disciplines were rehearsed long before the coronation, and they gave Haripal a steadiness of temper that would later be noted by every chronicler of Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior.

Ascension and the trials of succession
When the reign of Ruler Tomar dynasty Ancestor closed, Haripal was invested with the five symbols of the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior at Delhi (Dhillika), later Gwalior: the clan-tilak, the talismanic armour, the ancestral sword, the signet ring, and the turban of honour. The ceremonies were magnificent, but no sooner had the last hymn ended than the new ruler was tested. A group of feudatories - calculating on the sovereign's youth - withheld tribute. Others launched cattle-raids along the border. Still others opened secret correspondence with a neighbouring kingdom, hoping to carve out independent shares.
Haripal refused a hasty punitive war. Instead, a threefold policy was announced. Every rebel chief - without exception - received a personal letter, written in ink but sealed with the same signet that would later seal the punishment: it reaffirmed their ancient rights, welcomed them to the council, and invited them to the capital. Those who accepted were received with the same dignity they had known under Ruler Tomar dynasty Ancestor. Those who persisted in open rebellion were dealt with by a carefully chosen commander, with strict orders that the fields of ordinary cultivators should not be trampled and no market-town be looted. The families of the leading chiefs were also invited to send their sons to be trained in the royal court, as pages, cavalry officers, and scholars.
Within a single year the troubles collapsed. The border was sealed, the tribute-chests were full again, and even the most sceptical old chieftain admitted that Haripal had the two rarest qualities in a king: patience without softness, and resolution without cruelty. From this episode a new convention grew up within the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior: no loyal family would ever be displaced merely because the crown had changed hands.

Military campaigns, strategy, and the mark of valour
Under Haripal the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior army was reshaped into a far more cohesive instrument of war. The old feudal contingents were supplemented by standing regiments organised by arm: heavy infantry, bowmen, cavalry squadrons, elephant corps, batteries of light guns, companies of skirmishers, siege-engineering teams, and a dedicated espionage wing. Each of these was placed under a professional commandant reporting directly to Haripal, so that in a crisis blame could not travel down and credit could not travel up.
Campaigns such as “border-security expeditions”, “suppression of local uprisings” illustrate the methodical nature of that military mind. Before every major operation, reconnaissance parties travelled far ahead - disguised as mendicants, as grain-merchants, as cattle-drovers - counting the enemy's tents, inspecting the wells, watching the routes by which fodder and water reached their camps, and even counting the daily movements of their cavalry patrols. Only after that data had been compared with the reports of the astrologer, the priest performing the campaign-havan, the chief engineer, the field-hospital surgeon, and the paymaster would Haripal unfurl the royal standard.
Victory was never treated as a licence. Enemy kings who surrendered were guaranteed their lives, their families' safety, and often a place in the council of the victor. Wounded soldiers of the winning side received lifelong stipends; the families of the dead received rent-free lands and annual gifts. Even the war-horses and elephants were pensioned off in royal elephant-stables and stud-farms. The result was an army that fought for more than loot: it fought for the very name of Haripal.

Forts, roads, water, and the labour of building for posterity
The reign of Haripal was a long festival of building. “repair of the old capital fort”, “border outposts and village ponds” are the obvious and still-standing witnesses, but behind them lay an entire system. Every fort, large or small, was planned as a self-contained town: quarters for the royal family, barracks for the garrison, a shrine for Sri Krishna and the patron shrine of Gadh Govinda, houses for brahmin householders, huge granaries, dispensaries of herbal medicine, feeding-halls for the poor, and wells deep enough to withstand a siege of many years.
The road network was equally transformed. Between the principal towns, milestones, arched rest-houses, masonry step-wells, and roadside groves of shade-giving trees were set up at fixed intervals. Passes on the old caravan routes received small fortified outposts, so that merchants could move silver and spices without extra private guards. Market-places were laid out with proper lanes for separate trades, with overseers to keep weights and measures honest, grain-storehouses safe from damp, and the lanes free from encroachments.
Water management, however, was the most intimate form of building. In dry belts, johads, earthen dams, covered kunds, and lined tanks were constructed one after another. Canals drawn from the rivers began to reach villages that had always depended on the monsoon alone. Most importantly, traditional water-rights were written down for each village, witnessed by the chaupal, and registered by the royal clerk. So when drought came, the last peasant and the first thakur drew water by the same measure.

Administration, revenue, and the fundamentals of justice
Under Haripal the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior state was split into six clear departments: military, religious endowments, revenue and treasury, commerce and caravan tolls, land settlement, and water-forest stewardship. Each was placed under a senior minister whose registers were balanced every six months by Haripal personally, not by clerks alone. Beyond these, provincial governors for distant tracts were appointed for fixed terms, and required to submit written returns every lunar month.
The fiscal policy was deliberately mild. Taxes on agriculture were kept low; tolls on the long-distance routes were standardised so that a merchant could predict his costs from the first milestone; and hereditary classes engaged in public service - brahmins engaged in teaching and sacrifice, village teachers, cow-sanctuaries, hospitals, and pilgrim-hostels - were kept free of any impost. Embezzlement, however, was not. A corrupt officer was not merely transferred; the whole district was audited, the sums recovered, and the offender brought to the same open court that heard the poorest cultivator.
The jewel of the reign, however, was the visible even-handedness of justice. The proudest thakur and the most ragged cowherd stood before the same bench and under the same written rules. A public audience was held every single day, without exception, where every subject - irrespective of rank, wealth, or recommendation - could walk in and place a petition into the hands of Haripal. Hundreds of cases were settled by the ruler in person, with the full papers spread open on the carpet before them. It was this visible, daily, approachable justice that gave the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior regime a moral weight no mere army could ever buy.

Dharma, the arts, and the patronage of letters
Haripal was a devout ruler, yet never a sectarian one. Works such as “sustained worship of the clan deity”, “honours for local poets and musicians” made that policy visible across the entire kingdom. Temples, mosques, dargahs, and gurdwaras were all repaired; the ministers of every faith received allowances; cow-sanctuaries and hospitals for sick animals were maintained from the treasury; and dispensaries of Unani and Ayurvedic medicines were staffed by salaried physicians.
In the realm of art and craftsmanship, Haripal summoned masters of every school under royal protection. Architecture in stone, fresco-painting on plaster, stone-sculpture, perforated jalis, silver filigree, wood-carving, embroidery of cloth, beaten copper and brass, manuscript illumination, the forging of arms, and the exact science of fort-building - all were given workshops within the palace precincts, where apprentices learned the trade from masters in the old guru-shishya style.
Poets, bards, musicians, instrumentalists, and reciters of oral epic were given permanent stipends, seats of honour at festivals, and freedom to criticise the court as sharply as they pleased. As a result, folk literature flourished. Village-songs, bardic lays, khyals, nautch parties, and folk-plays picked up the memory of Haripal and carried it from the capital to the most remote hamlet. It was a cultural policy too often forgotten: true glory is not built from palaces alone, but from the voices of the people themselves.

Feudal loyalties, neighbouring states, and the diplomacy of moderation
Under Haripal, the compact between the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior throne and its feudatories was rewritten on the clearest possible terms. Each chief's ancient dignity, his land-rights, the honours due to his family at court, and the protection of his clan during minority successions - all were confirmed in a formal patent sealed by the crown. The leading chiefs were also given seats on the permanent war-council and the revenue council, so that policy was never made behind their backs.
Marriage alliances were also used with great care. Younger members of the royal family were linked by marriage to other ruling houses, not as a bribe, but as a public guarantee that quarrels of the past would not be revived. Friendly kingdoms were kept completely autonomous; defeated kingdoms were often given back their old ruling families, only under a treaty of friendship. No ancient line was displaced merely for the crime of having lost a battle.
These exact principles were also taught, with endless patience, to Next Ruler. For Haripal often said that a sword's edge fades in a single campaign, but a treaty well kept, kept by both sides for a whole lifetime, can outlast a hundred victories. It was this doctrine - not force alone - that extended the shadow of the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior far beyond its formal borders.

Character, daily discipline, and the living fountain of ideals
The day of Haripal was as regular as a temple bell. Awakening in the stillness before dawn, Haripal bathed, said the morning prayers, and visited the shrine of Sri Krishna and the patron shrine of Gadh Govinda with a simple offering. Then came a ride and weapons-drill, followed by a tour of the city - often in disguise, sometimes accompanied by one old bodyguard and no other retinue. In that disguise Haripal visited the grain markets, tasted the water at the public wells, sat in village schools, and listened to the women drawing water at the step-well. Nothing gave a truer picture of the kingdom.
The midday court was long, and grew longer when there were many petitions. Haripal never hurried a hearing. The youngest chowkidar's complaint outranked the longest minister's speech; a forged document was detected as often by the tone of the petitioner's voice as by the royal clerk's seals. One story has it that a small cultivator once came before the throne with a petition against a great chief, claiming his land had been seized. The chief produced sealed papers; Haripal studied them, sent a confidential commission to measure the actual fields, and then - in full court, before all the crown officers - restored the land to the cultivator and imposed a heavy fine on the chief. It became a byword: 'The court of Haripal is the only pilgrim centre where a poor man can hope to arrive first.'
In the evenings Haripal withdrew to the private library: Puranas, old chronicles, the aphorisms of Chanakya, grammar, poetics. Sometimes poets recited new compositions; sometimes instrumentalists played into the small hours. Popular traditions such as “that they were humble, just, and truly brave” still remember Haripal not as a triumphant warrior-king, but as a ruler who was gentle with the weak, immovable with the dishonest, and always, always, within reach of his people.

Mannaraja Tomar was born in the Jamuna-Chambal doab, and later the Gwalior tract north of the Vindhyas, a landscape where the memory of the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior was kept alive not by stone inscriptions alone, but by bards who walked from village to village, by mothers who sang lullabies of old battles, and by clan-councils held under the ancient banyan. 1516–1518 CE was an age when every fort had its own ghost, every pass its own tradition, and every shrine its own protective vow. The clan deity, Sri Krishna and the patron shrine of Gadh Govinda, was worshipped with a lamp that never went out; caravans stopped before entering the hills; and sentinels watched every waterhole through the night. It was in such a world that Mannaraja Tomar grew up, sitting at the knee of Ruler Tomar dynasty Ancestor and learning the first, cruel truth of Rajput kingship: that the throne is not comfort, but a vow.
Their education was deliberately rounded. The four martial sciences - bow, horse, sword, and mace - were taught before the letters of the alphabet. Then came the shastras, but never only from books. Economics was taught from the account-books of a merchant caravan. Statecraft was taught from a rebel chieftain's forgiven letter. Justice was taught from the actual hearing of a widow's land dispute in the village chaupal. Music and painting were not ornaments; they were meant to train eye and ear, so that a king could read the lie in a courtier's salute and the truth in the murmur of a crowd.
From the queen-mother, Mannaraja Tomar received an even more difficult lesson: a king's courage is not proven on the battlefield alone. It is proven when he listens silently to a complaint he does not want to hear, when he feeds the hungry before his own table, when he keeps his word to a weaker ally even if every minister advises him otherwise. These quiet disciplines were rehearsed long before the coronation, and they gave Mannaraja Tomar a steadiness of temper that would later be noted by every chronicler of Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior.

Ascension and the trials of succession
When the reign of Ruler Tomar dynasty Ancestor closed, Mannaraja Tomar was invested with the five symbols of the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior at Delhi (Dhillika), later Gwalior: the clan-tilak, the talismanic armour, the ancestral sword, the signet ring, and the turban of honour. The ceremonies were magnificent, but no sooner had the last hymn ended than the new ruler was tested. A group of feudatories - calculating on the sovereign's youth - withheld tribute. Others launched cattle-raids along the border. Still others opened secret correspondence with a neighbouring kingdom, hoping to carve out independent shares.
Mannaraja Tomar refused a hasty punitive war. Instead, a threefold policy was announced. Every rebel chief - without exception - received a personal letter, written in ink but sealed with the same signet that would later seal the punishment: it reaffirmed their ancient rights, welcomed them to the council, and invited them to the capital. Those who accepted were received with the same dignity they had known under Ruler Tomar dynasty Ancestor. Those who persisted in open rebellion were dealt with by a carefully chosen commander, with strict orders that the fields of ordinary cultivators should not be trampled and no market-town be looted. The families of the leading chiefs were also invited to send their sons to be trained in the royal court, as pages, cavalry officers, and scholars.
Within a single year the troubles collapsed. The border was sealed, the tribute-chests were full again, and even the most sceptical old chieftain admitted that Mannaraja Tomar had the two rarest qualities in a king: patience without softness, and resolution without cruelty. From this episode a new convention grew up within the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior: no loyal family would ever be displaced merely because the crown had changed hands.

Military campaigns, strategy, and the mark of valour
Under Mannaraja Tomar the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior army was reshaped into a far more cohesive instrument of war. The old feudal contingents were supplemented by standing regiments organised by arm: heavy infantry, bowmen, cavalry squadrons, elephant corps, batteries of light guns, companies of skirmishers, siege-engineering teams, and a dedicated espionage wing. Each of these was placed under a professional commandant reporting directly to Mannaraja Tomar, so that in a crisis blame could not travel down and credit could not travel up.
Campaigns such as “border-security expeditions”, “suppression of local uprisings” illustrate the methodical nature of that military mind. Before every major operation, reconnaissance parties travelled far ahead - disguised as mendicants, as grain-merchants, as cattle-drovers - counting the enemy's tents, inspecting the wells, watching the routes by which fodder and water reached their camps, and even counting the daily movements of their cavalry patrols. Only after that data had been compared with the reports of the astrologer, the priest performing the campaign-havan, the chief engineer, the field-hospital surgeon, and the paymaster would Mannaraja Tomar unfurl the royal standard.
Victory was never treated as a licence. Enemy kings who surrendered were guaranteed their lives, their families' safety, and often a place in the council of the victor. Wounded soldiers of the winning side received lifelong stipends; the families of the dead received rent-free lands and annual gifts. Even the war-horses and elephants were pensioned off in royal elephant-stables and stud-farms. The result was an army that fought for more than loot: it fought for the very name of Mannaraja Tomar.

Forts, roads, water, and the labour of building for posterity
The reign of Mannaraja Tomar was a long festival of building. “repair of the old capital fort”, “border outposts and village ponds” are the obvious and still-standing witnesses, but behind them lay an entire system. Every fort, large or small, was planned as a self-contained town: quarters for the royal family, barracks for the garrison, a shrine for Sri Krishna and the patron shrine of Gadh Govinda, houses for brahmin householders, huge granaries, dispensaries of herbal medicine, feeding-halls for the poor, and wells deep enough to withstand a siege of many years.
The road network was equally transformed. Between the principal towns, milestones, arched rest-houses, masonry step-wells, and roadside groves of shade-giving trees were set up at fixed intervals. Passes on the old caravan routes received small fortified outposts, so that merchants could move silver and spices without extra private guards. Market-places were laid out with proper lanes for separate trades, with overseers to keep weights and measures honest, grain-storehouses safe from damp, and the lanes free from encroachments.
Water management, however, was the most intimate form of building. In dry belts, johads, earthen dams, covered kunds, and lined tanks were constructed one after another. Canals drawn from the rivers began to reach villages that had always depended on the monsoon alone. Most importantly, traditional water-rights were written down for each village, witnessed by the chaupal, and registered by the royal clerk. So when drought came, the last peasant and the first thakur drew water by the same measure.

Administration, revenue, and the fundamentals of justice
Under Mannaraja Tomar the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior state was split into six clear departments: military, religious endowments, revenue and treasury, commerce and caravan tolls, land settlement, and water-forest stewardship. Each was placed under a senior minister whose registers were balanced every six months by Mannaraja Tomar personally, not by clerks alone. Beyond these, provincial governors for distant tracts were appointed for fixed terms, and required to submit written returns every lunar month.
The fiscal policy was deliberately mild. Taxes on agriculture were kept low; tolls on the long-distance routes were standardised so that a merchant could predict his costs from the first milestone; and hereditary classes engaged in public service - brahmins engaged in teaching and sacrifice, village teachers, cow-sanctuaries, hospitals, and pilgrim-hostels - were kept free of any impost. Embezzlement, however, was not. A corrupt officer was not merely transferred; the whole district was audited, the sums recovered, and the offender brought to the same open court that heard the poorest cultivator.
The jewel of the reign, however, was the visible even-handedness of justice. The proudest thakur and the most ragged cowherd stood before the same bench and under the same written rules. A public audience was held every single day, without exception, where every subject - irrespective of rank, wealth, or recommendation - could walk in and place a petition into the hands of Mannaraja Tomar. Hundreds of cases were settled by the ruler in person, with the full papers spread open on the carpet before them. It was this visible, daily, approachable justice that gave the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior regime a moral weight no mere army could ever buy.

Dharma, the arts, and the patronage of letters
Mannaraja Tomar was a devout ruler, yet never a sectarian one. Works such as “sustained worship of the clan deity”, “honours for local poets and musicians” made that policy visible across the entire kingdom. Temples, mosques, dargahs, and gurdwaras were all repaired; the ministers of every faith received allowances; cow-sanctuaries and hospitals for sick animals were maintained from the treasury; and dispensaries of Unani and Ayurvedic medicines were staffed by salaried physicians.
In the realm of art and craftsmanship, Mannaraja Tomar summoned masters of every school under royal protection. Architecture in stone, fresco-painting on plaster, stone-sculpture, perforated jalis, silver filigree, wood-carving, embroidery of cloth, beaten copper and brass, manuscript illumination, the forging of arms, and the exact science of fort-building - all were given workshops within the palace precincts, where apprentices learned the trade from masters in the old guru-shishya style.
Poets, bards, musicians, instrumentalists, and reciters of oral epic were given permanent stipends, seats of honour at festivals, and freedom to criticise the court as sharply as they pleased. As a result, folk literature flourished. Village-songs, bardic lays, khyals, nautch parties, and folk-plays picked up the memory of Mannaraja Tomar and carried it from the capital to the most remote hamlet. It was a cultural policy too often forgotten: true glory is not built from palaces alone, but from the voices of the people themselves.

Feudal loyalties, neighbouring states, and the diplomacy of moderation
Under Mannaraja Tomar, the compact between the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior throne and its feudatories was rewritten on the clearest possible terms. Each chief's ancient dignity, his land-rights, the honours due to his family at court, and the protection of his clan during minority successions - all were confirmed in a formal patent sealed by the crown. The leading chiefs were also given seats on the permanent war-council and the revenue council, so that policy was never made behind their backs.
Marriage alliances were also used with great care. Younger members of the royal family were linked by marriage to other ruling houses, not as a bribe, but as a public guarantee that quarrels of the past would not be revived. Friendly kingdoms were kept completely autonomous; defeated kingdoms were often given back their old ruling families, only under a treaty of friendship. No ancient line was displaced merely for the crime of having lost a battle.
These exact principles were also taught, with endless patience, to Next Ruler. For Mannaraja Tomar often said that a sword's edge fades in a single campaign, but a treaty well kept, kept by both sides for a whole lifetime, can outlast a hundred victories. It was this doctrine - not force alone - that extended the shadow of the Tomar of Delhi and Gwalior far beyond its formal borders.

The day of Mannaraja Tomar was as regular as a temple bell. Awakening in the stillness before dawn, Mannaraja Tomar bathed, said the morning prayers, and visited the shrine of Sri Krishna and the patron shrine of Gadh Govinda with a simple offering. Then came a ride and weapons-drill, followed by a tour of the city - often in disguise, sometimes accompanied by one old bodyguard and no other retinue. In that disguise Mannaraja Tomar visited the grain markets, tasted the water at the public wells, sat in village schools, and listened to the women drawing water at the step-well. Nothing gave a truer picture of the kingdom.
The midday court was long, and grew longer when there were many petitions. Mannaraja Tomar never hurried a hearing. One story has it that a small cultivator once came before the throne with a petition against a great chief, claiming his land had been seized. It became a byword: 'The court of Mannaraja Tomar is the only pilgrim centre where a poor man can hope to arrive first.'
In the evenings Mannaraja Tomar withdrew to the private library: Puranas, old chronicles, the aphorisms of Chanakya, grammar, poetics. Sometimes poets recited new compositions; sometimes instrumentalists played into the small hours. Popular traditions such as “that they were humble, just, and truly brave” still remember Mannaraja Tomar not as a triumphant warrior-king, but as a ruler who was gentle with the weak, immovable with the dishonest, and always, always, within reach of his people.

bhima-deva-i-solanki.story:
Early life and the depth of lineage
Bhimadeva I was born in the Sabarmati basin and the uplands of medieval Gujarat, a landscape where the memory of the Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat was kept alive not by stone inscriptions alone, but by bards who walked from village to village, by mothers who sang lullabies of old battles, and by clan-councils held under the ancient banyan. 1022-1064 CE was an age when every fort had its own ghost, every pass its own tradition, and every shrine its own protective vow. The clan deity, Sri Somnath and the reverence of Sri Ambika, was worshipped with a lamp that never went out; caravans stopped before entering the hills; and sentinels watched every waterhole through the night. It was in such a world that Bhimadeva I grew up, sitting at the knee of Ruler Durlabharaja and learning the first, cruel truth of Rajput kingship: that the throne is not comfort, but a vow.
Their education was deliberately rounded. The four martial sciences - bow, horse, sword, and mace - were taught before the letters of the alphabet. Then came the shastras, but never only from books. Economics was taught from the account-books of a merchant caravan. Statecraft was taught from a rebel chieftain's forgiven letter. Justice was taught from the actual hearing of a widow's land dispute in the village chaupal. Music and painting were not ornaments; they were meant to train eye and ear, so that a king could read the lie in a courtier's salute and the truth in the murmur of a crowd.
From the queen-mother, Bhimadeva I received an even more difficult lesson: a king's courage is not proven on the battlefield alone. It is proven when he listens silently to a complaint he does not want to hear, when he feeds the hungry before his own table, when he keeps his word to a weaker ally even if every minister advises him otherwise. These quiet disciplines were rehearsed long before the coronation, and they gave Bhimadeva I a steadiness of temper that would later be noted by every chronicler of Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat.

Ascension and the trials of succession
When the reign of Ruler Durlabharaja closed, Bhimadeva I was invested with the five symbols of the Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat at Anahilapataka (Patan): the clan-tilak, the talismanic armour, the ancestral sword, the signet ring, and the turban of honour. The ceremonies were magnificent, but no sooner had the last hymn ended than the new ruler was tested. A group of feudatories - calculating on the sovereign's youth - withheld tribute. Others launched cattle-raids along the border. Still others opened secret correspondence with a neighbouring kingdom, hoping to carve out independent shares.
Bhimadeva I refused a hasty punitive war. Instead, a threefold policy was announced. Every rebel chief - without exception - received a personal letter, written in ink but sealed with the same signet that would later seal the punishment: it reaffirmed their ancient rights, welcomed them to the council, and invited them to the capital. Those who accepted were received with the same dignity they had known under Ruler Durlabharaja. Those who persisted in open rebellion were dealt with by a carefully chosen commander, with strict orders that the fields of ordinary cultivators should not be trampled and no market-town be looted. The families of the leading chiefs were also invited to send their sons to be trained in the royal court, as pages, cavalry officers, and scholars.
Within a single year the troubles collapsed. The border was sealed, the tribute-chests were full again, and even the most sceptical old chieftain admitted that Bhimadeva I had the two rarest qualities in a king: patience without softness, and resolution without cruelty. From this episode a new convention grew up within the Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat: no loyal family would ever be displaced merely because the crown had changed hands.

Military campaigns, strategy, and the mark of valour
Under Bhimadeva I the Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat army was reshaped into a far more cohesive instrument of war. The old feudal contingents were supplemented by standing regiments organised by arm: heavy infantry, bowmen, cavalry squadrons, elephant corps, batteries of light guns, companies of skirmishers, siege-engineering teams, and a dedicated espionage wing. Each of these was placed under a professional commandant reporting directly to Bhimadeva I, so that in a crisis blame could not travel down and credit could not travel up.
Campaigns such as “Reconstruction after the Somnath raid”, “Struggle against raiders on the western coast”, “Resistance to Malwa-Chalukya pressure” illustrate the methodical nature of that military mind. Before every major operation, reconnaissance parties travelled far ahead - disguised as mendicants, as grain-merchants, as cattle-drovers - counting the enemy's tents, inspecting the wells, watching the routes by which fodder and water reached their camps, and even counting the daily movements of their cavalry patrols. Only after that data had been compared with the reports of the astrologer, the priest performing the campaign-havan, the chief engineer, the field-hospital surgeon, and the paymaster would Bhimadeva I unfurl the royal standard.
Victory was never treated as a licence. Enemy kings who surrendered were guaranteed their lives, their families' safety, and often a place in the council of the victor. Wounded soldiers of the winning side received lifelong stipends; the families of the dead received rent-free lands and annual gifts. Even the war-horses and elephants were pensioned off in royal elephant-stables and stud-farms. The result was an army that fought for more than loot: it fought for the very name of Bhimadeva I.

Forts, roads, water, and the labour of building for posterity
The reign of Bhimadeva I was a long festival of building. “Strengthening of coastal defence posts” are the obvious and still-standing witnesses, but behind them lay an entire system. Every fort, large or small, was planned as a self-contained town: quarters for the royal family, barracks for the garrison, a shrine for Sri Somnath and the reverence of Sri Ambika, houses for brahmin householders, huge granaries, dispensaries of herbal medicine, feeding-halls for the poor, and wells deep enough to withstand a siege of many years.
The road network was equally transformed. Between the principal towns, milestones, arched rest-houses, masonry step-wells, and roadside groves of shade-giving trees were set up at fixed intervals. Passes on the old caravan routes received small fortified outposts, so that merchants could move silver and spices without extra private guards. Market-places were laid out with proper lanes for separate trades, with overseers to keep weights and measures honest, grain-storehouses safe from damp, and the lanes free from encroachments.
Water management, however, was the most intimate form of building. In dry belts, johads, earthen dams, covered kunds, and lined tanks were constructed one after another. Canals drawn from the rivers began to reach villages that had always depended on the monsoon alone. Most importantly, traditional water-rights were written down for each village, witnessed by the chaupal, and registered by the royal clerk. So when drought came, the last peasant and the first thakur drew water by the same measure.

Administration, revenue, and the fundamentals of justice
Under Bhimadeva I the Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat state was split into six clear departments: military, religious endowments, revenue and treasury, commerce and caravan tolls, land settlement, and water-forest stewardship. Each was placed under a senior minister whose registers were balanced every six months by Bhimadeva I personally, not by clerks alone. Beyond these, provincial governors for distant tracts were appointed for fixed terms, and required to submit written returns every lunar month.
The fiscal policy was deliberately mild. Taxes on agriculture were kept low; tolls on the long-distance routes were standardised so that a merchant could predict his costs from the first milestone; and hereditary classes engaged in public service - brahmins engaged in teaching and sacrifice, village teachers, cow-sanctuaries, hospitals, and pilgrim-hostels - were kept free of any impost. Embezzlement, however, was not. A corrupt officer was not merely transferred; the whole district was audited, the sums recovered, and the offender brought to the same open court that heard the poorest cultivator.
The jewel of the reign, however, was the visible even-handedness of justice. The proudest thakur and the most ragged cowherd stood before the same bench and under the same written rules. A public audience was held every single day, without exception, where every subject - irrespective of rank, wealth, or recommendation - could walk in and place a petition into the hands of Bhimadeva I. Hundreds of cases were settled by the ruler in person, with the full papers spread open on the carpet before them. It was this visible, daily, approachable justice that gave the Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat regime a moral weight no mere army could ever buy.

Dharma, the arts, and the patronage of letters
Bhimadeva I was a devout ruler, yet never a sectarian one. Works such as “Patronised temple restoration”, “Expanded agriculture and irrigation” made that policy visible across the entire kingdom. Temples, mosques, dargahs, and gurdwaras were all repaired; the ministers of every faith received allowances; cow-sanctuaries and hospitals for sick animals were maintained from the treasury; and dispensaries of Unani and Ayurvedic medicines were staffed by salaried physicians.
In the realm of art and craftsmanship, Bhimadeva I summoned masters of every school under royal protection. Architecture in stone, fresco-painting on plaster, stone-sculpture, perforated jalis, silver filigree, wood-carving, embroidery of cloth, beaten copper and brass, manuscript illumination, the forging of arms, and the exact science of fort-building - all were given workshops within the palace precincts, where apprentices learned the trade from masters in the old guru-shishya style.
Poets, bards, musicians, instrumentalists, and reciters of oral epic were given permanent stipends, seats of honour at festivals, and freedom to criticise the court as sharply as they pleased. As a result, folk literature flourished. Village-songs, bardic lays, khyals, nautch parties, and folk-plays picked up the memory of Bhimadeva I and carried it from the capital to the most remote hamlet. It was a cultural policy too often forgotten: true glory is not built from palaces alone, but from the voices of the people themselves.

Under Bhimadeva I, the compact between the Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat throne and its feudatories was rewritten on the clearest possible terms. The leading chiefs were also given seats on the permanent war-council and the revenue council, so that policy was never made behind their backs.
Marriage alliances were also used with great care. Younger members of the royal family were linked by marriage to other ruling houses, not as a bribe, but as a public guarantee that quarrels of the past would not be revived. Friendly kingdoms were kept completely autonomous; defeated kingdoms were often given back their old ruling families, only under a treaty of friendship. No ancient line was displaced merely for the crime of having lost a battle.
These exact principles were also taught, with endless patience, to Karna Deva I. For Bhimadeva I often said that a sword's edge fades in a single campaign, but a treaty well kept, kept by both sides for a whole lifetime, can outlast a hundred victories. It was this doctrine - not force alone - that extended the shadow of the Solanki (Chaulukya) of Gujarat far beyond its formal borders.

The day of Bhimadeva I was as regular as a temple bell. Nothing gave a truer picture of the kingdom.

The youngest chowkidar's complaint outranked the longest minister's speech; a forged document was detected as often by the tone of the petitioner's voice as by the royal clerk's seals. The border was sealed, the tribute-chests were full again, and even the most sceptical old chieftain admitted that Madho Singh I (Kota) had the two rarest qualities in a king: patience without softness, and resolution without cruelty. From this episode a new convention grew up within the Hada Chauhan of Bundi and Kota: no loyal family would ever be displaced merely because the crown had changed hands.

Military campaigns, strategy, and the mark of valour
Under Madho Singh I (Kota) the Hada Chauhan of Bundi and Kota army was reshaped into a far more cohesive instrument of war. The old feudal contingents were supplemented by standing regiments organised by arm: heavy infantry, bowmen, cavalry squadrons, elephant corps, batteries of light guns, companies of skirmishers, siege-engineering teams, and a dedicated espionage wing. Each of these was placed under a professional commandant reporting directly to Madho Singh I (Kota), so that in a crisis blame could not travel down and credit could not travel up.
Campaigns such as “Regional service in Mughal campaigns” illustrate the methodical nature of that military mind. Before every major operation, reconnaissance parties travelled far ahead - disguised as mendicants, as grain-merchants, as cattle-drovers - counting the enemy's tents, inspecting the wells, watching the routes by which fodder and water reached their camps, and even counting the daily movements of their cavalry patrols. Only after that data had been compared with the reports of the astrologer, the priest performing the campaign-havan, the chief engineer, the field-hospital surgeon, and the paymaster would Madho Singh I (Kota) unfurl the royal standard.
Victory was never treated as a licence. Enemy kings who surrendered were guaranteed their lives, their families' safety, and often a place in the council of the victor. Wounded soldiers of the winning side received lifelong stipends; the families of the dead received rent-free lands and annual gifts. Even the war-horses and elephants were pensioned off in royal elephant-stables and stud-farms. The result was an army that fought for more than loot: it fought for the very name of Madho Singh I (Kota).

Forts, roads, water, and the labour of building for posterity
The reign of Madho Singh I (Kota) was a long festival of building. “Kotagarh (early work)” are the obvious and still-standing witnesses, but behind them lay an entire system. Every fort, large or small, was planned as a self-contained town: quarters for the royal family, barracks for the garrison, a shrine for Sri Ajinkya Mata and the ancestral Hada shrines, houses for brahmin householders, huge granaries, dispensaries of herbal medicine, feeding-halls for the poor, and wells deep enough to withstand a siege of many years.
The road network was equally transformed. Between the principal towns, milestones, arched rest-houses, masonry step-wells, and roadside groves of shade-giving trees were set up at fixed intervals. Passes on the old caravan routes received small fortified outposts, so that merchants could move silver and spices without extra private guards. Market-places were laid out with proper lanes for separate trades, with overseers to keep weights and measures honest, grain-storehouses safe from damp, and the lanes free from encroachments.
Water management, however, was the most intimate form of building. In dry belts, johads, earthen dams, covered kunds, and lined tanks were constructed one after another. Canals drawn from the rivers began to reach villages that had always depended on the monsoon alone. Most importantly, traditional water-rights were written down for each village, witnessed by the chaupal, and registered by the royal clerk. So when drought came, the last peasant and the first thakur drew water by the same measure.

Administration, revenue, and the fundamentals of justice
Under Madho Singh I (Kota) the Hada Chauhan of Bundi and Kota state was split into six clear departments: military, religious endowments, revenue and treasury, commerce and caravan tolls, land settlement, and water-forest stewardship. Each was placed under a senior minister whose registers were balanced every six months by Madho Singh I (Kota) personally, not by clerks alone. Beyond these, provincial governors for distant tracts were appointed for fixed terms, and required to submit written returns every lunar month.
The fiscal policy was deliberately mild. Taxes on agriculture were kept low; tolls on the long-distance routes were standardised so that a merchant could predict his costs from the first milestone; and hereditary classes engaged in public service - brahmins engaged in teaching and sacrifice, village teachers, cow-sanctuaries, hospitals, and pilgrim-hostels - were kept free of any impost. Embezzlement, however, was not. A corrupt officer was not merely transferred; the whole district was audited, the sums recovered, and the offender brought to the same open court that heard the poorest cultivator.
The jewel of the reign, however, was the visible even-handedness of justice. The proudest thakur and the most ragged cowherd stood before the same bench and under the same written rules. A public audience was held every single day, without exception, where every subject - irrespective of rank, wealth, or recommendation - could walk in and place a petition into the hands of Madho Singh I (Kota). Hundreds of cases were settled by the ruler in person, with the full papers spread open on the carpet before them. It was this visible, daily, approachable justice that gave the Hada Chauhan of Bundi and Kota regime a moral weight no mere army could ever buy.

Dharma, the arts, and the patronage of letters
Madho Singh I (Kota) was a devout ruler, yet never a sectarian one. Works such as “Developed administration and architecture in Kota” made that policy visible across the entire kingdom. Temples, mosques, dargahs, and gurdwaras were all repaired; the ministers of every faith received allowances; cow-sanctuaries and hospitals for sick animals were maintained from the treasury; and dispensaries of Unani and Ayurvedic medicines were staffed by salaried physicians.
In the realm of art and craftsmanship, Madho Singh I (Kota) summoned masters of every school under royal protection. Architecture in stone, fresco-painting on plaster, stone-sculpture, perforated jalis, silver filigree, wood-carving, embroidery of cloth, beaten copper and brass, manuscript illumination, the forging of arms, and the exact science of fort-building - all were given workshops within the palace precincts, where apprentices learned the trade from masters in the old guru-shishya style.
Poets, bards, musicians, instrumentalists, and reciters of oral epic were given permanent stipends, seats of honour at festivals, and freedom to criticise the court as sharply as they pleased. As a result, folk literature flourished. Village-songs, bardic lays, khyals, nautch parties, and folk-plays picked up the memory of Madho Singh I (Kota) and carried it from the capital to the most remote hamlet. It was a cultural policy too often forgotten: true glory is not built from palaces alone, but from the voices of the people themselves.

Feudal loyalties, neighbouring states, and the diplomacy of moderation
Under Madho Singh I (Kota), the compact between the Hada Chauhan of Bundi and Kota throne and its feudatories was rewritten on the clearest possible terms. Each chief's ancient dignity, his land-rights, the honours due to his family at court, and the protection of his clan during minority successions - all were confirmed in a formal patent sealed by the crown. The leading chiefs were also given seats on the permanent war-council and the revenue council, so that policy was never made behind their backs.
Marriage alliances were also used with great care. Younger members of the royal family were linked by marriage to other ruling houses, not as a bribe, but as a public guarantee that quarrels of the past would not be revived. Friendly kingdoms were kept completely autonomous; defeated kingdoms were often given back their old ruling families, only under a treaty of friendship. No ancient line was displaced merely for the crime of having lost a battle.
These exact principles were also taught, with endless patience, to the Hada rulers of Kota. For Madho Singh I (Kota) often said that a sword's edge fades in a single campaign, but a treaty well kept, kept by both sides for a whole lifetime, can outlast a hundred victories. It was this doctrine - not force alone - that extended the shadow of the Hada Chauhan of Bundi and Kota far beyond its formal borders.

Character, daily discipline, and the living fountain of ideals
The day of Madho Singh I (Kota) was as regular as a temple bell. Awakening in the stillness before dawn, Madho Singh I (Kota) bathed, said the morning prayers, and visited the shrine of Sri Ajinkya Mata and the ancestral Hada shrines with a simple offering. Then came a ride and weapons-drill, followed by a tour of the city - often in disguise, sometimes accompanied by one old bodyguard and no other retinue. In that disguise Madho Singh I (Kota) visited the grain markets, tasted the water at the public wells, sat in village schools, and listened to the women drawing water at the step-well. Nothing gave a truer picture of the kingdom.
The midday court was long, and grew longer when there were many petitions. Madho Singh I (Kota) never hurried a hearing. The youngest chowkidar's complaint outranked the longest minister's speech; a forged document was detected as often by the tone of the petitioner's voice as by the royal clerk's seals. One story has it that a small cultivator once came before the throne with a petition against a great chief, claiming his land had been seized. The chief produced sealed papers; Madho Singh I (Kota) studied them, sent a confidential commission to measure the actual fields, and then - in full court, before all the crown officers - restored the land to the cultivator and imposed a heavy fine on the chief. It became a byword: 'The court of Madho Singh I (Kota) is the only pilgrim centre where a poor man can hope to arrive first.'
In the evenings Madho Singh I (Kota) withdrew to the private library: Puranas, old chronicles, the aphorisms of Chanakya, grammar, poetics. Sometimes poets recited new compositions; sometimes instrumentalists played into the small hours. Popular traditions such as “Founding of Kota state and urban development” still remember Madho Singh I (Kota) not as a triumphant warrior-king, but as a ruler who was gentle with the weak, immovable with the dishonest, and always, always, within reach of his people.
